messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Firefighter
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 45

**Patient Vignette: "Elena"**

Elena is a 26-year-old single woman who has been a firefighter for the past three years. She presents as physically strong and alert, her posture rigid even in the soft chair of my office. She speaks in a clipped, efficient tone, as if delivering a report over a radio. She is here because her captain told her she would be placed on light duty if she didn't "get her head checked out." She agreed, but she does not believe talking will help.

The story she tells begins fourteen months ago. She and her partner responded to a call for a structure fire in a condemned warehouse. They were doing a primary search on the second floor when the floor collapsed beneath her. She fell into a basement storage room, landing hard on concrete. Her radio was shattered. Her leg was pinned under a collapsed steel beam. She was alone, in the dark, with the sound of fire crackling above her and the smell of smoke and something chemical burning. She was trapped for six hours.

During those hours, she thought she would die. She screamed for help until her voice gave out. She tried to move the beam until her hands bled. She remembers the silence between the crashes of debris, the way the darkness pressed against her eyes. She remembers bargaining with God, a God she had never believed in. She remembers the moment she stopped screaming and just waited. She was not rescued; she was discovered. A thermal imaging camera caught her heat signature. When they pulled her out, she was hypothermic, dehydrated, and in shock.

Now, fourteen months later, the world has changed. She no longer sleeps in her own bed. She sleeps on the floor of her living room, her back against the wall, so she can see the only door. She keeps a hall light on. She cannot tolerate being in any room without a visible exit. She has stopped going to the grocery store because the aisles feel like corridors. She has stopped dating because the thought of being in a man's apartment, in a room with a closed door, sends her heart into a gallop.

At work, she is a liability. She can still fight a fire from the outside, but she refuses to go interior. The last time she was ordered to make entry, she froze at the threshold. Her captain saw her face and pulled her back. She now drives the truck. She feels the shame of this like a hot brand. She sees the looks from the younger firefighters, the ones who don't know. She tells herself she is a coward.

Her thoughts are consumed by the event. She replays the fall, the impact, the dark. She has nightmares where the beam is not a beam but a person, holding her down. She startles at loud noises, at the smell of smoke, at the feeling of a room getting too warm. She has stopped cooking with gas. She has stopped lighting candles. She avoids basements, elevators, and any room without a window.

She tells me she is fine. She says the past is the past. But her body tells a different story. She sits with her fists clenched, her jaw tight, her eyes darting to the door every few seconds. She is a prisoner of a room she is no longer in. She is still waiting to be found.
